2. Suppose the following data comes from a study on plant growth (mm) where 2 plants are in
each pot, 3 pots are within each plot and 2 plots are given one of two fertilizer treatments.
```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="75%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("Screenshot 2026-09-18 193422.png")
```
____________________________________________________________________________________________________
(a) Arrange the data into a dataframe so that it can be analysed. Print out this dataframe.
R code:
```{r Question_2 (a)}
library(knitr)

# Input the 24 plant growth measurements (2 plants per pot, 3 pots per plot, 2 plots, 2 treatments)
Growth <- c(14.6, 15.2, 13.2, 12.9, 16.4, 12.2,  # Treatment 1, Plot 1
            18.5, 16.7, 22.2, 18.8, 24.7, 20.3,  # Treatment 1, Plot 2
            7.1,  7.7,  6.8,  6.0,  10.0, 8.3,   # Treatment 2, Plot 1
            9.7,  8.8,  6.8,  9.0,  10.4, 11.3)  # Treatment 2, Plot 2

# Create corresponding categorical factors for the experimental design
Treatment <- factor(rep(c("Treatment 1", "Treatment 2"), each = 12))
Plot <- factor(rep(rep(c("Plot 1", "Plot 2"), each = 6), times = 2))
Pot <- factor(rep(rep(c("Pot 1", "Pot 2", "Pot 3"), each = 2), times = 4))

# Combine into a data frame and display it as an elegant table
plant_data <- data.frame(Treatment, Plot, Pot, Growth)
kable(plant_data, caption = "Plant Growth Data Frame")

```
____________________________________________________________________________________________________
(b) Sort the data by plant growth.
R code:
```{r Question_2 (b)}
sorted_data <- plant_data[order(plant_data$Growth), ]
kable(sorted_data, caption = "Sorted Plant Growth Data")

```

(c) Calculate the mean, and standard deviation of the data.
R code:
```{r Question_2 (c)}
mean_growth <- mean(plant_data$Growth)
sd_growth   <- sd(plant_data$Growth)

# Create a tidy summary data frame for a professional look
summary_stats <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Mean Growth (mm)", "Standard Deviation (mm)"),

)

# Display as a clean table using kable
kable(summary_stats, caption = "Summary Statistics for Plant Growth")
```

bin sizes of 2 mm.

```{r Question_2 (d)}
     breaks = seq(4, 26, by = 2),

     border = "white",
     add = TRUE)

```

3. Write a function that uses the short cut formula to calculate the sample variance of a data vector. Use the vector y=(11,11,10,8,11,3,15,11,7,6) as your test vector.
R code:
```{r Question_3}
library(knitr)

# Define a function to calculate sample variance using the short-cut formula
# Formula: s^2 = [ sum(y^2) - (sum(y))^2 / n ] / (n - 1)
calc_sample_var <- function(y) {
  n <- length(y)
  sum_y <- sum(y)
  sum_y2 <- sum(y^2)
  
  # Calculate sample variance
  var_value <- (sum_y2 - (sum_y^2) / n) / (n - 1)
  
  return(var_value)
}

# Test vector given in the assignment
y_test <- c(11, 11, 10, 8, 11, 3, 15, 11, 7, 6)

# Apply our custom function to the test vector
custom_var <- calc_sample_var(y_test)

# Compare with R's built-in var() function for verification
builtin_var <- var(y_test)

# Create a tidy data frame to display the results cleanly in the PDF
variance_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Custom Short-Cut Function", "Built-in var() Function"),
  Sample_Variance = c(round(custom_var, 4), round(builtin_var, 4))
)

# Display as an elegant table
kable(variance_results, caption = "Comparison of Sample Variance Calculations")

```

4. On the course webpage you will find a dataset with filename ‘tv.txt’. The data arise from a
study examining the time teenagers spend watching tv. A random sample of n = 100 eighth
grade American high school students was obtained, and the number of minutes spent watching
TV during the first week of October was recorded. A similar sample of m = 90 Canadian
students was also obtained. In this study it is of interest to compare the TV watching habits of
the teenagers from the two different countries, specifically to determine if Canadian students
watch less TV than their American counterparts.

(a) Compare the two samples using appropriate descriptive statistics, including side-by-side
boxplots.
R code:
```{r Question_4 (a)}
library(knitr)

# Load the data, treating "NA" as missing values
tv_data <- read.table("tv.txt", header = TRUE, na.strings = "NA")

# Calculate comprehensive summary statistics for both countries
summary_stats_tv <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Sample Size (n)", "Mean", "Standard Deviation", "Median", "Min", "Max"),
  Canada = c(
    sum(!is.na(tv_data$Canada)),
    round(mean(tv_data$Canada, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(sd(tv_data$Canada, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(median(tv_data$Canada, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(min(tv_data$Canada, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(max(tv_data$Canada, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
  ),
  US = c(
    sum(!is.na(tv_data$US)),
    round(mean(tv_data$US, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(sd(tv_data$US, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(median(tv_data$US, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(min(tv_data$US, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    round(max(tv_data$US, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
  )
)

# Display the summary statistics as an elegant table
kable(summary_stats_tv, caption = "Summary Statistics of TV Viewing Time (Canada vs. US)")

# Create professional side-by-side boxplots to compare the distributions
par(mar = c(5, 5, 4, 2) + 0.1) # Adjust plot margins

boxplot(tv_data$Canada, tv_data$US,
        names = c("Canada", "US"),
        main = "Comparison of TV Viewing Time",
        ylab = "TV Viewing Time",
        col = c("#5C93C4", "#E08283"), # Different pleasant colors for each group
        border = "gray30",
        las = 1,
        cex.main = 1.2,
        cex.lab = 1.1)

# Add background grid lines for better readability
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "gray90", lty = "dashed")

# Redraw boxplots on top of the grid lines
boxplot(tv_data$Canada, tv_data$US,
        names = c("Canada", "US"),
        col = c("#5C93C4", "#E08283"),
        border = "gray30",
        add = TRUE,
        las = 1)

```

(b) Write an R function z.test(y1,y2,H1) to compute the p-value for a large sample z-test
(discussed in lecture) for testing equality of two population means (H0 : µ1 = µ2).
The arguments to this function are: y1, a vector containing the sample measurements
from the first population; y2, a vector containing the sample measurements from the
second population; and H1, a string variable, which takes one of three possible values:
‘two.sided’, ‘less’ or ‘greater’ specifying the alternative hypothesis. To complete this
question you will need to use the R function pnorm() which computes standard normal
probabilities, see the help file ?pnorm.

R code:
```{r Question_4 (b)}

z.test <- function(y1, y2, H1) {
  # Remove missing values (NA) 
  y1 <- na.omit(y1)
  y2 <- na.omit(y2)
  
  # Sample sizes
  n1 <- length(y1)
  n2 <- length(y2)
  
  # Sample means and standard deviations
  mean1 <- mean(y1)
  mean2 <- mean(y2)
  sd1 <- sd(y1)
  sd2 <- sd(y2)
  
  # Standard error of the difference between two means
  se <- sqrt((sd1^2 / n1) + (sd2^2 / n2))
  
  # Calculate the Z test statistic 
  z_stat <- (mean1 - mean2) / se
  
  # Calculate the p-value based on the specified alternative hypothesis (H1)
  if (H1 == "two.sided") {
    p_val <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_stat)))
  } else if (H1 == "less") {
    p_val <- pnorm(z_stat)
  } else if (H1 == "greater") {
    p_val <- 1 - pnorm(z_stat)
  } else {
    stop("Invalid H1 argument. Use 'two.sided', 'less', or 'greater'.")
  }
  
  # Return a clean list that contain the z-statistic and p-value
  results <- list(
    z_statistic = z_stat,
    p_value = p_val,
    H1 = H1
  )
  
  return(results)
}
```

____________________________________________________________________________________________________
(c) Apply your function to the TV data, computing the p-values for each of the three possible
alternative hypotheses.
R code:
```{r Question_4 (c)}
# Apply the function with the three required H1 arguments
test_two_sided <- z.test(tv_data$Canada, tv_data$US, H1 = "two.sided")
test_less      <- z.test(tv_data$Canada, tv_data$US, H1 = "less")
test_greater   <- z.test(tv_data$Canada, tv_data$US, H1 = "greater")

# Compile the results into a clean data frame
z_test_results <- data.frame(
  Alternative_Hypothesis = c("Two-sided (Canada != US)", 
                             "Less (Canada < US)", 
                             "Greater (Canada > US)"),
  
  Z_Statistic = c(round(test_two_sided$z_statistic, 4), 
                  round(test_less$z_statistic, 4), 
                  round(test_greater$z_statistic, 4)),
  
  P_Value = c(format.pval(test_two_sided$p_value, digits = 4, eps = 1e-4),
              format.pval(test_less$p_value, digits = 4, eps = 1e-4),
              format.pval(test_greater$p_value, digits = 4, eps = 1e-4))
)

# Display the results using kable
kable(z_test_results, caption = "Z-Test Results for TV Viewing Time (Canada vs. US)")
```

(d) Which of the three alternative hypotheses is relevant for the particular question being
asked in this study? Comment on the results.

R code:

```{r Question_4 (d)}

# Extract the p-value for the 'less' alternative
p_val_less <- test_less$p_value

# Print a formatted statement for the report
cat("The p-value for the one-sided test (Canada < US) is:", format.pval(p_val_less, digits = 4))
```

Conclusion:

Based on the research question: "Do Canadian students watch less TV than US students?" The 

appropriate alternative hypothesis is "less" (Canada < US).

To test whether Canadian students watch less television than US students, we set up the Hypotheses

Null Hypothesis ($H_0$): 
$\mu_{\text{Canada}} \ge \mu_{\text{US}}$

Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$): 
$\mu_{\text{Canada}} < \mu_{\text{US}}$ (corresponding to alternative = "less").

Based on the two-sample z-test performed using our custom function, the resulting p-value is 

evaluated against the standard significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$. If the p-value is less than 

$0.05$, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is statistically significant evidence 

that Canadian students watch less TV on average than US students. Otherwise, we fail to reject the 

null hypothesis.
